analytes.name: Ferritin

labRange.source: Mayo Clinic Laboratories, test FERR1 (female 18 to 50 years; ≥51 years: 11 to 328)

analytes.origin: The Mayo female reference interval of 6 to 175 µg/L is a statistical range for apparently healthy adults; the catalogue cites textbook chapters only (Henry’s, 2007; Tietz, 2012 and 2018) and no reference-interval study [S1]. The Mayo text states that ferritin shows no sex difference before puberty and that female values rise with age [S1]. Labcorp reports 15 to 150 ng/mL for adult women but states that it “has adopted a threshold of 30 ng/mL in adult and adolescent patients, to identify patients with iron deficiency” [S2].

sexSpecific.what: WHO 2020 threshold for risk of iron overload in apparently healthy individuals (>150 µg/L in menstruating women; >200 µg/L in men and non-menstruating women). The WHO iron-deficiency threshold (<15 µg/L from 5 years of age) is identical for both sexes.

contested.summary: The WHO <15 µg/L threshold is expert opinion graded as low certainty; its evidence review found a mean ferritin of 15.1 µg/L (9 studies, 390 participants) where bone-marrow iron was absent [S4]. In 7,498 non-pregnant women aged 15 to 49 (NHANES), Mei et al. (2021) found that haemoglobin began to decline below a ferritin of 25.2 µg/L (95% CI 24.2 to 26.2) and soluble transferrin receptor to rise below 24.0 µg/L (23.3 to 24.6); at this threshold the US prevalence of iron deficiency in premenopausal women would rise from about 17% to about 30% [S5, S6]. The British Society of Gastroenterology (2021) states that values below 30 µg/L “are generally indicative of low body iron stores” and that a 45 µg/L threshold has specificity 0.92 [S7]; the American Society of Hematology (2026) raised its diagnostic threshold to 30 ng/mL irrespective of anaemia, with 50 ng/mL in higher-risk groups, as reported in secondary accounts of the guideline; the threshold values were not verified against the full text [S11, S12].

analytes.guidanceInBand: The British Society of Gastroenterology (2021) states: “SF levels of less than 30 µg/L are generally indicative of low body iron stores”; “The cancer risk in iron deficiency without anaemia is low”; and “There is insufficient evidence to support invasive investigation in non-anaemic iron deficiency” [S7]. WHO (2020) states that, with infection or inflammation, “a ferritin concentration below 30 μg/L in children and 70 μg/L in adults may be used to indicate iron deficiency” [S4].

analytes.name: Haemoglobin

labRange.source: Mayo Clinic Laboratories, test CBC (≥18 years)

analytes.origin: For its complete blood count (CBC) intervals, Mayo cites Adeli et al. (2015), a CALIPER and Canadian Health Measures Survey study of 11,999 participants aged 3 to 79 measured on Beckman Coulter HmX and Sysmex analysers, which found that “females had lower hemoglobin and hematocrit starting at puberty” [H1, H3]. The WHO anaemia thresholds (120 g/L in women, 130 g/L in men) were first proposed in 1968 on the basis of “four published references and one set of unpublished observations” in European and North American populations; the WHO 2024 revision retained them, basing the adult values on fifth centiles of apparently healthy, iron-replete populations [H4].

sexSpecific.what: WHO 2024 haemoglobin threshold defining anaemia in non-pregnant women and men aged 15 to 65 (120 and 130 g/L); the CDC 1998 thresholds are 12.0 and 13.5 g/dL.

contested.summary: Beutler and Waalen (2006) excluded iron deficiency (transferrin saturation <16% or ferritin <10 µg/L) in 2,966 white women aged 20 to 49 and 6,709 white men aged 20 to 59 (Scripps-Kaiser), and a sex difference persisted: fifth centiles were 12.2 and 13.7 g/dL respectively [H5]. Braat et al. (2024), the WHO-commissioned pooled analysis, reported fifth centiles of 119.7 g/L (90% CI 119.1 to 120.3; n=3,640) in iron-replete non-pregnant women and 134.9 g/L (134.2 to 135.6; n=2,377) in men; WHO retained 120 g/L for women, and retained 130 g/L for men despite data “suggest[ing] a higher haemoglobin cutoff (i.e. 135 g/L)” [H4, H6]. Rushton et al. (2001) argued that the female reference limit had been derived from iron-deficient populations; the iron-replete data of Morison and Ferguson (ferritin 80 to 100 µg/L; 612 men, 1,327 women) showed 10th centiles of 139 and 123 g/L respectively and that a male reference range would misclassify 25 to 50% of women as anaemic [H10, H10a].

analytes.guidanceInBand: WHO (2024) classifies 110 to 119 g/L in a non-pregnant woman as “Mild anaemia” and notes that management “could vary depending on the clinical scenario and the underlying cause(s)” [H4]. The British Society of Gastroenterology (2021) states: “iron deficiency should be confirmed by iron studies prior to investigation. Serum ferritin is the single most useful marker of IDA” [H9].

analytes.name: Haematocrit

labRange.source: Mayo Clinic Laboratories, test CBC (≥18 years)

analytes.origin: As for haemoglobin, Mayo cites Adeli et al. (2015; Canadian Health Measures Survey, 11,999 participants aged 3 to 79) and the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) reference-interval standard EP28-A3c; Adeli et al. reported lower haematocrit in female participants from puberty [H1, H3]. The interval is a population centile, not an outcome-based threshold.

sexSpecific.what: CDC 1998 haematocrit threshold for anaemia in non-pregnant women and men aged 18 years and over (5th percentile of NHANES III after exclusion of probable iron deficiency). The WHO 2024 guideline gives haemoglobin thresholds only.

contested.summary: No haematocrit-specific threshold study was identified; the dispute derives from haemoglobin, for which iron-replete fifth centiles retain a sex difference (Beutler and Waalen, 2006; Braat et al., 2024) [H5, H6]. The range of disagreement is narrow: the Mayo female lower reference limit (35.5%) lies immediately below the CDC anaemia threshold (35.7%), so a value of 35.6% falls within the Mayo reference interval and below the CDC threshold [H1, H8].

analytes.guidanceInBand: CDC (1998) classifies a haematocrit below 35.7% in a non-pregnant woman as anaemia and states that a ferritin of 15 µg/L or less then “confirms iron deficiency in anemic women” [H8]. Mayo states: “Results should be interpreted in conjunction with the patient’s clinical picture and appropriate additional testing performed” [H1].

analytes.name: Transferrin saturation

labRange.source: Mayo Clinic Laboratories, test SFEC (percent saturation; serum iron is sex-specific: male 50 to 150, female 35 to 145 mcg/dL)

analytes.origin: The Mayo interval of 14 to 50% is supported by textbook and guideline citations only (Tietz, 7th ed., 2023; the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) 2019 haemochromatosis guideline; Lopez et al., Lancet, 2016), with no reference-interval study cited; Mayo reports day-to-day intra-individual variation of “approximately 25% to 30%” and states that the test “should not be used as the primary test for iron deficiency” [T1]. The deficiency thresholds in use (16% and 20%) are conventions and not sex-partitioned centiles [T1, T4, T5].

sexSpecific.what: EASL 2022 transferrin saturation above which iron overload is suspected and HFE genotyping is recommended (with ferritin >200 µg/L in women and >300 µg/L in men). The iron-deficiency thresholds (<16%, CDC; <20%, BSG, and in the presence of inflammation) are identical for both sexes.

contested.summary: The Mayo reference interval begins at 14%, below both the CDC iron-deficiency threshold (<16%) and the <20% threshold of the British Society of Gastroenterology and of Mayo in inflammation; a value of 15 to 19% therefore falls within the laboratory reference interval while meeting a deficiency definition [T1, T4, T5]. The European Association for the Study of the Liver states “There is no universally accepted threshold for ferritin or transferrin saturation indicating iron overload” and adopts the sex-specific 45% and 50% values from a single population screening study [T3].

analytes.guidanceInBand: Mayo states: “Percent saturation less than 16% is generally used to screen for iron deficiency, but a threshold of 20% is used in the presence of inflammation” [T1]. The British Society of Gastroenterology (2021) states: “A transferrin saturation of <20% is indicative of iron restriction” and “Transferrin saturation can help if a false-normal ferritin is suspected” [T5].

analytes.name: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)

labRange.source: Mayo Clinic Laboratories, test CBC (≥18 years; identical for men and women)

analytes.origin: Mayo cites Adeli et al. (2015; Canadian Health Measures Survey, 11,999 participants aged 3 to 79, Beckman Coulter HmX or Sysmex analysers) and Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) EP28-A3c; unlike haemoglobin and haematocrit, the adult MCV interval is not partitioned by sex [M1, M3]. Mayo defines microcytosis as MCV <80 fL [M1].

sexSpecific.what: No sex-specific MCV threshold was identified in WHO, CDC or BSG documents; CDC defines low MCV as a value below the age-specific 5th percentile of NHANES III and reports no sex-specific values [M4].

contested.summary: No published argument that the female MCV reference interval is derived from an inappropriate population was identified. The sole discrepancy is definitional: the Mayo lower reference limit (78.2 fL) differs from its microcytosis threshold (80 fL) [M1].

analytes.guidanceInBand: Mayo states: “Anemias are characterized as microcytic (MCV <80), macrocytic (MCV >100), or normocytic” and “iron deficiency anemia is characterized by a high RDW, while thalassemia is characterized by a low RDW” [M1]. The British Society of Gastroenterology (2021) states: “Age, sex, Hb concentration and mean cell volume are all independent predictors of risk of GI cancer in IDA” [M5].

analytes.name: High-sensitivity troponin I (Abbott ARCHITECT/Alinity)

labRange.source: Abbott ARCHITECT STAT High Sensitive Troponin-I package insert (outside the US, April 2015), as tabulated by IFCC C-CB v05/2023; the US insert (September 2019) gives 17, 35 and 28 ng/L (female, male, overall)

analytes.origin: The 99th-percentile limits are manufacturer values derived by a robust statistic from 1,531 apparently healthy participants aged 21 to 75 years (764 women, 766 men); troponin was measurable in 78% of the women [S5]. An independent re-derivation in the American Association for Clinical Chemistry (AACC) Universal Sample Bank (340 healthy women after exclusions) gave a lower female 99th percentile of 13 ng/L, with troponin measurable in 42% of women, and showed that stricter health exclusions lowered the limit [S6].

sexSpecific.what: 99th-percentile upper reference limit defining myocardial injury; the thresholds used in the High-STEACS trial

contested.summary: With a single contemporary-assay threshold, type 1 myocardial infarction (MI) was diagnosed in 11% of women and 19% of men; with the high-sensitivity assay and sex-specific thresholds, in 22% of women and 21% of men. Of the 56 reclassified women, 25% had died or had a reinfarction at 12 months and 2% underwent angiography [S1]. In the High-STEACS trial (48,282 patients), 1,470 of 1,771 reclassified patients (83%) were women and myocardial injury in women increased by 42% (3,521 to 4,991), but implementation of the sex-specific thresholds was not associated with a lower rate of MI or cardiovascular death at 1 year in reclassified patients (15% in the validation phase and 12% in the implementation phase; adjusted odds ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.61) [S2][S3]. In England in 2019, 54 of 97 trusts reporting a threshold used sex-specific thresholds [S7].

analytes.guidanceInBand: The Fourth Universal Definition states that “Detection of an elevated cTn value above the 99th percentile URL is defined as myocardial injury” and that “sex-specific 99th percentile URLs are recommended for hs-cTn assays”; acute myocardial infarction additionally requires “a rising and/or falling pattern of cTn values with at least one value above the 99th percentile URL” with evidence of ischaemia [S4].

analytes.name: High-sensitivity troponin T (Roche Elecsys)

labRange.source: University of Iowa Hospitals pathology handbook (Roche US 5th-generation hs-TnT; same values as the Roche US Gen 5 package insert in the IFCC table). The EU insert gives 9, 17 and 14 ng/L (female, male, overall); NHS Lothian reports 1 to 9 ng/L (female) and 1 to 16 ng/L (male)

analytes.origin: Roche’s EU 99th-percentile limits (overall 14, women 9, men 17 ng/L) were derived from 533 participants aged 20 to 71 years, with troponin measurable in 49.7% of the women; the US Gen 5 values (19, 14 and 22 ng/L respectively) were derived from 1,301 participants aged 21 to 89 years [S5]. In the American Association for Clinical Chemistry (AACC) Universal Sample Bank, high-sensitivity troponin T was measurable in 16 to 21% of healthy women and the female 99th percentile was 10 to 11 ng/L [S6]. Outside the US, most laboratories use the single 14 ng/L limit [S6][S8].

sexSpecific.what: 99th-percentile upper reference limit defining myocardial injury (EU package insert; the US Gen 5 insert gives 14 and 22 ng/L)

contested.summary: The Fourth Universal Definition recommends sex-specific 99th percentiles for all high-sensitivity assays [S4], but Roche released only a combined 14 ng/L threshold outside the US; in an international survey, 12 of 12 institutions using high-sensitivity troponin T applied the combined value, whereas 5 of 6 using high-sensitivity troponin I applied sex-specific thresholds [S8]. In England, where the Roche assay was used in 57% of trusts, 54 of 97 trusts reporting a threshold used sex-specific values in 2019 [S7]. The High-STEACS outcome evidence [S1][S2][S3] was generated with the Abbott assay, not the Roche assay.

analytes.guidanceInBand: The Fourth Universal Definition states that “Significantly lower values are observed among women compared with men” and that “sex-specific 99th percentile URLs are recommended for hs-cTn assays”, while noting that “there is controversy as to whether this approach provides valuable additional information” [S4].

analytes.name: Creatinine (serum) and eGFR

labRange.source: Labcorp test 001370 (kinetic Jaffe), ages ≥15 years; attributed to “Labcorp internal studies”

analytes.origin: Labcorp attributes its sex-partitioned interval only to “Labcorp internal studies”, with no population or year stated [S11]; ARUP publishes no interval (“By report”) [S12]. Creatinine production depends on muscle mass: in 170 healthy adults, lean mass predicted serum creatinine but not cystatin C [S16]. The eGFR equation encodes sex with κ = 0.7 (female) versus 0.9 (male), α = −0.241 versus −0.302, and a multiplier of 1.012 for women; it was fitted on 8,254 participants (43.7% female) [S14][S15].

sexSpecific.what: CKD-EPI 2021 female sex multiplier (with sex-specific κ 0.7/0.9 and α −0.241/−0.302, female/male) in the eGFR equation

contested.summary: In a woman with low muscle mass, creatinine may lie within the female reference interval (0.57 to 1.00 mg/dL) while filtration is reduced, because creatinine reflects muscle mass as well as GFR [S16]; the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) 2024 guideline names “reduced muscle mass” as a reason to prefer cystatin C-based eGFR [S17]. The female interval itself is documented only as “internal studies” [S11]. No study quantifying under-detection of chronic kidney disease in women attributable to the female interval was identified.

analytes.guidanceInBand: The Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guideline states: “We recommend using eGFRcr-cys in clinical situations when eGFRcr is less accurate and GFR affects clinical decision-making (1C)” and “Consider eGFRcys rather than eGFRcr-cys in otherwise healthy populations with decreased creatinine generation due to reduced muscle mass” [S17].

analytes.name: NT-proBNP

labRange.source: University of Iowa Hospitals pathology handbook, ages 19 to 44 years (95th percentiles in patients without congestive heart failure; rising with age: women 65 to 74 years 0 to 353 pg/mL, men 65 to 74 years 0 to 229 pg/mL); the value for both sexes is the ESC 2021 non-acute upper limit of normal

analytes.origin: The 125 pg/mL rule-out threshold is the upper limit of normal in the non-acute setting stated by the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) [S19], a single value for both sexes. In 18,356 participants in Scotland without cardiovascular disease, median (97.5th percentile) NT-proBNP was higher in women than in men in younger adults and lower at the oldest ages: 51 (196) pg/mL in women and 21 (104) pg/mL in men under 30 years of age, 66 (299) and 38 (195) pg/mL at 50 to 59 years, and 240 (2,704) and 281 (6,792) pg/mL at 80 years or over [S20]. Sex-partitioned hospital reference intervals (for example, Iowa) give women a higher upper limit than men below 75 years of age [S18].

sexSpecific.what: No guideline sex-specific threshold; the ESC applies NT-proBNP <125 pg/mL (BNP <35 pg/mL) to all adults

contested.summary: NT-proBNP ≥125 pg/mL was present in 9.8% of women and 1.4% of men under 30 years of age, and in 76.5% of women and 81.0% of men aged 80 years or over; across the cohort the adjusted odds ratio for women relative to men was 9.48 (95% CI 5.60 to 16.1). The authors stated that “An NT-proBNP ≥125 pg/mL is common in females without classical cardiovascular risk factors” and called for age- and sex-specific thresholds [S20]. In the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study, absolute risk at guideline thresholds was lower in White women and higher in Black men [S21]. In younger adults the direction of misclassification is over-identification of women without heart failure, the opposite of that for troponin.

analytes.guidanceInBand: The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) states that “A plasma concentration of … NT-proBNP <125 pg/mL … make a diagnosis of HF unlikely”; above this value echocardiography is advised, with the caveat that elevated natriuretic peptides have causes including “AF, increasing age, and acute or chronic kidney disease” [S19].

analytes.name: Creatine kinase (CK)

labRange.source: Labcorp test 001362, ages 18 to 50 years (kinetic, 340 nm); no source cited

analytes.origin: Labcorp states no provenance for its CK intervals [S22]. Population-derived 97.5th percentiles are higher: 207 U/L in women in the Tromsø Study (n = 6,904 after exclusions) [S23]; 295 U/L in white women and 487 U/L in Black women in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2011 to 2014 (n = 10,096) [S25]. In Amsterdam, limits were 2 to 5 times the manufacturer’s, and 49% of participants of African descent exceeded the manufacturer’s limits [S24].

sexSpecific.what: Laboratory upper reference limit (Labcorp, ages 18 to 50 years); no guideline-set sex-specific threshold exists

contested.summary: Each population study cited places the female 97.5th percentile above the 182 U/L laboratory limit: 207 U/L in Norway [S23], and 295 U/L in white and 487 U/L in Black US women [S25]. Ancestry has a larger effect than sex partitioning accounts for: odds ratios for elevated CK were 5.08 in Black women and 8.39 in Black men, and body composition did not explain the difference [S25]; in Amsterdam, 49% of participants of African descent exceeded the manufacturer’s limit [S24].

analytes.guidanceInBand: No society guideline statement on sex-specific interpretation of CK was identified. The authors of the Amsterdam study concluded that “The variation in CK activity within the population is wider than previously suggested” and that raising the upper reference limit “may improve the use of statins” [S24].

The disease thresholds have a different origin: urate crystallises above its saturation point, and the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) defines asymptomatic hyperuricaemia “as an SU concentration of ≥6.8 mg/dl” (SU, serum urate) [S28]; treatment targets of <6 mg/dL (ACR; European League Against Rheumatism, EULAR) are set below saturation so that crystals dissolve [S28][S29].

sexSpecific.what: No sex-specific guideline threshold: the ACR and EULAR targets (<6 mg/dL; EULAR <5 mg/dL in severe gout) and the ≥6.8 mg/dL definition of hyperuricaemia apply to both sexes; only laboratory reference intervals are sex-partitioned

contested.summary: The female laboratory interval is a population distribution, not a risk threshold, and for older women (upper limits 7.2 and 7.9 mg/dL) it extends above both the 6 mg/dL treatment target and the 6.8 mg/dL saturation-based definition of hyperuricaemia [S27][S28]. In the Framingham cohort (2,476 women; 104 incident gout cases among them), gout risk in women rose in a graded manner with urate, although less steeply than in men [S30]. The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) notes that “Gout has differential impact on patients by sex”, but its patient panel comprised eight men [S28].

analytes.guidanceInBand: The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) states that “Initiating ULT is conditionally recommended against in patients with asymptomatic hyperuricemia” (≥6.8 mg/dL without flares or tophi); for diagnosed gout, “we strongly recommend continuing ULT to achieve and maintain an SU target of <6 mg/dl over no target” [S28]. The European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) target is “<6 mg/dL (360 µmol/L) and <5 mg/dL (300 µmol/L) in those with severe gout” [S29]. ULT denotes urate-lowering therapy; SU, serum urate.

analytes.name: ALT (alanine aminotransferase)

labRange.source: LabCorp (female <33, male <45 U/L, adults aged 18 and over); ARUP reports 5 to 50 U/L “by report”; Leeds NHS adults <=40 U/L (not sex-specific); RCPA/AACB harmonised male 5 to 40, female 5 to 35 U/L

analytes.origin: Laboratory limits are conventionally the central 95% of a “healthy” reference group; for ALT, such groups historically included individuals with undiagnosed fatty liver and were assembled without regard to BMI, and a survey of 67 laboratories in one US state found upper reference limits from 31 to 72 U/L, set variously from manufacturer inserts, local controls or textbooks [S2]. LabCorp derived its current limits (female <33, male <45 U/L) from an internal study of more than 260,000 subjects and cites Prati et al. (2002) as a reason for lowering them [S4]; the Leeds NHS trust uses a Siemens insert traced to a 2000 textbook [S7]; the Australasian harmonised limits (male 40, female 35 U/L) were confirmed against 1,876 healthy adults [S9].

sexSpecific.what: ACG 2017 “true healthy normal” upper limit of ALT (range quoted as 19 to 25 U/L in women, 29 to 33 U/L in men); higher values should be assessed

contested.summary: Prati et al. (2002), in 6,835 screened blood donors in Milan, set the 95th-percentile upper reference limit at 30 U/L in men and 19 U/L in women against the then-current 40 and 30 U/L; the new limits raised sensitivity for HCV viraemia from 55% to 76.3% [S1]. Ruhl and Everhart (2012), in NHANES (3,747 low-risk versus 259 HCV-positive participants), found optimal cut-offs of 29 U/L in men and 22 U/L in women, which would classify 28.3% of US women as “elevated” [S3]. The American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) 2017 guideline adopted 19 to 25 U/L for women, whereas laboratories still report upper limits of 33 to 50 U/L, and the 2021 repetition of the Prati study (21,296 donors) with an assay standardised to the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (IFCC) method gave 30 U/L for women because the standardised assay yields higher values [S10, S11].

analytes.guidanceInBand: The American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) 2017 guideline states: “A normal ALT should be <29-33 IU/l in males and 19-25 IU/l in females. Minimal elevations may be approached by a history and examination, discontinuation of hepatotoxic medicines and all alcohol consumption, in addition to an evaluation for hemochromatosis, fatty liver and viral hepatitis.” A borderline elevation is “<2X ULN”; for levels below 5 times the upper reference limit, the history and tests “should assess for viral hepatitis B and C, alcoholic and NAFLD, hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, alpha-1-anti-trypsin deficiency, autoimmune hepatitis and consider drugs/supplement related injury” (strong recommendation, very low level of evidence) [S2].

labRange.source: LabCorp (4.8 to 5.6%; prediabetes 5.7 to 6.4%; diabetes >=6.5%); Leeds NHS <42 mmol/mol, diabetes >48 mmol/mol

analytes.origin: These are diagnostic decision thresholds, not population reference intervals. The American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care 2026 define diabetes in Table 2.1 as “A1C >=6.5% (>=48 mmol/mol)” and prediabetes in Table 2.2 as “A1C 5.7-6.4% (39-47 mmol/mol)”, and require an NGSP-certified assay standardised to the DCCT [S18]; the Leeds NHS trust uses the WHO 2011 limit of 48 mmol/mol and a local non-diabetic cut-off of <42 mmol/mol [S7]. The ADA notes that “Black individuals have slightly higher A1C levels (approximately 0.3%)” and that in conditions with altered red cell turnover, pregnancy, some haemoglobin variants, G6PD deficiency and HIV, “plasma glucose criteria should be used to diagnose diabetes” [S18].

sexSpecific.what: No guideline or laboratory consulted sets a sex-specific HbA1c threshold

contested.summary: Holland et al. (2024), in 146,907 UK adults with a single test (replicated in 938,678 from six laboratories), found that women under 50 had a mean HbA1c of 34.4 versus 36.0 mmol/mol in men (1.6 mmol/mol lower, p < 0.0001; 0.9 mmol/mol at 50 and over); the authors modelled lowering the diagnostic cut-off from 48 to 46 mmol/mol (6.5% to 6.4%) for women under 50, estimated that 34,953 additional women in England and Wales would be reclassified, and attributed the difference to “menstruation and hence shorter erythrocyte survival” (about 4% of circulating blood, approximately 1.9 mmol/mol) [S21]. The mechanism is inferred, and no guideline has adopted a sex-specific cut-off.

analytes.guidanceInBand: The American Diabetes Association (ADA) 2026 standards define prediabetes as “A1C 5.7-6.4% (39-47 mmol/mol)” and diabetes as “A1C >=6.5% (>=48 mmol/mol)”; in the absence of unequivocal hyperglycaemia a confirmatory test is required [S18]. LabCorp states “Prediabetes: 5.7% to 6.4%” and that patients with prediabetes should be retested yearly [S19].

analytes.name: HDL cholesterol

labRange.source: LabCorp (>39 mg/dL, one interval for all); University of Washington Medicine reports male >=40, female >=50 mg/dL

analytes.origin: The National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel III (NCEP ATP III, 2001) raised “categorical low HDL cholesterol from <35 mg/dL to <40 mg/dL because the latter is a better measure of a depressed HDL” and set it “both in men and women” [S22, S23]. The panel explained that women “typically have higher HDL cholesterol levels than men”, so that <40 mg/dL identifies “approximately one-third of men and about one-fifth of women”, and that “Setting a different cutpoint for categorical low HDL cholesterol for men and women was rejected because it would make many women who are otherwise at low risk eligible for LDL-lowering drugs”; instead, “<50 mg/dL” was made “a marginal risk factor in women”, used only in the metabolic syndrome definition [S23]. The LabCorp limit of “>39” reproduces the ATP III categorical value for all patients [S27].

sexSpecific.what: Low HDL-C criterion for the metabolic syndrome (ATP III Table 8: men <40 mg/dL, women <50 mg/dL; three of five criteria establish the diagnosis)

contested.summary: The Adult Treatment Panel III (ATP III) report records that the female cut-point was a policy compromise: <50 mg/dL was “rejected” as a categorical risk factor to avoid making “many women who are otherwise at low risk eligible for LDL-lowering drugs”, and retained only as a “marginal risk factor” in the metabolic syndrome criteria [S23]. Laboratories in turn report a single limit (LabCorp >39 mg/dL for all [S27]; University of Washington, female >=50 mg/dL [S30]); a value of 45 mg/dL in a woman falls within the reference interval of the first and below the lower reference limit of the second. In the BioCycle study, HDL also varied with the cycle, from a median of 48 mg/dL at menses to 52 mg/dL at ovulation (“HDL levels were highest around ovulation”) [S24]. The current European Society of Cardiology/European Atherosclerosis Society (ESC/EAS) 2019 guideline sets no HDL goal: “To date, no specific goals for HDL-C or TG levels have been determined in clinical trials” and HDL-raising therapies “do not reduce the risk of ASCVD” [S31]; according to Agarwala et al. (2020) [S33], the women-specific additions of the 2018 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) guideline are risk enhancers (premature menopause, pre-eclampsia), not an HDL threshold (reported in a secondary source; guideline full text not verified).

analytes.guidanceInBand: The Adult Treatment Panel III (ATP III) does not count a value in this band as a risk factor (“Low HDL cholesterol (<40 mg/dL)”) [S22], but “for women, HDL cholesterol <50 mg/dL counts as one indicator in the diagnosis of the metabolic syndrome”, “a marginal risk factor in women, which will mandate more intensive lifestyle therapies (weight reduction and increased physical activity)” [S23]; metabolic syndrome is diagnosed “when three or more of the risk determinants shown in Table 8 are present” [S22]. The European Society of Cardiology/European Atherosclerosis Society (ESC/EAS) 2019 guideline sets no HDL-C goal [S31].

analytes.name: TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone)

labRange.source: LabCorp test 004259 (above 10 years, ECLIA); ARUP test 0070145 reports 0.27 to 4.20 mU/L at 20 years and over.

analytes.origin: The 0.4 to 4.5 mIU/L group of reference intervals derives from NHANES III (1988 to 1994): of 17,353 United States residents aged 12 years and over, 16,533 were “disease-free” and 13,344 formed a “reference population” after exclusion of pregnancy, hormone use, positive thyroid antibodies and biochemical dysfunction [S3]. The disease-free upper reference limit was 4.5 mIU/L and the reference-population interval 0.45 to 4.12 mIU/L, as stated in the 2012 guideline of the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and the American Thyroid Association [S4]. No interval was derived separately for women, although TSH was higher and antibody positivity more common in women [S3].

sexSpecific.what: Pregnancy only: the American Thyroid Association 2017 upper reference limit is approximately 4.0 mU/L (about 0.5 mU/L below the non-pregnant limit) from weeks 7 to 12 where no local trimester-specific interval exists; no laboratory or guideline consulted gives a sex-specific interval for non-pregnant adults. By age, the 97.5th centile was 3.56 mIU/L at 20 to 29 years and 7.49 mIU/L at 80 years and over.

contested.summary: The upper reference limit “has not been universally accepted”: proposals of 2.5 or 3.0 mIU/L rest on the right skew of the reference distribution (values of 3.1 to 4.12 mIU/L) and a median near 1.5 mIU/L [S4]; the 2003 “0.3-3.0” proposal of the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists is reported in secondary sources only [S10]. Opponents of these proposals note that 85% of the NHANES III reference group had TSH below 2.5 mIU/L and that lowering the limit would add “more than 10 million additional diagnoses” per year [S4, S5]. A 2019 BMJ guideline (21 trials, 2,192 participants) recommends strongly against treating subclinical hypothyroidism, except for women planning pregnancy, patients with TSH above 20 mIU/L or severe symptoms, and young adults [S12].

analytes.guidanceInBand: Recommendation 16 of the 2012 guideline of the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and the American Thyroid Association (ATA) states: “Treatment based on individual factors for patients with TSH levels between the upper limit of a given laboratory's reference range and 10 mIU/L should be considered particularly if patients have symptoms suggestive of hypothyroidism, positive TPOAb or evidence of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease” [S4]; for TSH of 2.5 to 4.5 mIU/L, “there are virtually no clinical outcome data to support treating” [S4]. In pregnancy, Recommendation 29 of the ATA 2017 guideline states that levothyroxine “may be considered” for thyroid peroxidase antibody (TPOAb)-positive women with TSH above 2.5 mU/L and below the upper limit of the pregnancy interval, and is “not recommended” for TPOAb-negative women with TSH within the pregnancy interval “or < 4.0 mU/L if unavailable” [S6].

analytes.name: Vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D)

labRange.source: ARUP test 2002348 (LC-MS/MS, adults 18 years and over): “Optimum level 30-80 ng/mL”; deficiency below 20 ng/mL; insufficiency 20 to 29 ng/mL.

analytes.origin: The laboratory categories reproduce the Endocrine Society 2011 scheme: deficiency “below 20 ng/ml”, insufficiency “21-29 ng/ml” and sufficiency “30-100 ng/ml” [S3]. The Institute of Medicine (IOM) 2011 Dietary Reference Intakes report, from the same bone data, set 16 ng/mL (40 nmol/L) as the average requirement and 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) as the concentration at which “Practically all persons are sufficient” [S2]. Neither threshold was derived by sex; the IOM Estimated Average Requirement and Recommended Dietary Allowance for vitamin D are the same for men and women [S2].

sexSpecific.what: No sex-specific 25(OH)D threshold appears in the Institute of Medicine 2011, Endocrine Society 2011 or 2024, US Preventive Services Task Force 2021 or UK Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition 2016 documents. The Endocrine Society 2024 guideline suggests empiric supplementation in pregnancy without a threshold [S4].

contested.summary: Institute of Medicine (IOM) committee members responded in 2012 to “aspects of The Endocrine Society guideline that are not well supported” [S6]; the Endocrine Society 2024 guideline “no longer endorses the target 25(OH)D level of 30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L)” and no longer endorses “specific 25(OH)D levels to define vitamin D sufficiency” [S4]. The IOM value of 20 ng/mL is a population coverage value (97.5% of people), not an individual decision threshold, with the average requirement at 16 ng/mL [S2]. The US Preventive Services Task Force (2021) states that “no one serum vitamin D level cutpoint defines deficiency” and that evidence for screening is insufficient [S9]. The UK Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition uses 25 nmol/L (10 ng/mL) as a population protective level and states that it “is not a clinical threshold diagnostic of the disease” [S7].

analytes.guidanceInBand: The Endocrine Society 2011 guideline defines “vitamin D insufficiency as a 25(OH)D of 21-29 ng/ml” [S3]. The Institute of Medicine 2011 report states: “Practically all persons are sufficient at serum 25OHD levels of at least 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL)” [S2]. The Endocrine Society 2024 guideline states: “In healthy adults, we suggest against routine screening for 25(OH)D levels”; it “suggests against empiric vitamin D supplementation above the current DRI” (Dietary Reference Intake) for adults under 75 years, while suggesting empiric supplementation at 75 years and over and “during pregnancy” [S4].

analytes.name: Testosterone, total (women)

labRange.source: ARUP test 0081058 (LC-MS/MS): premenopausal women 18 years and over 9 to 55 ng/dL; postmenopausal women 5 to 32 ng/dL; men 18 to 39 years 300 to 1080 ng/dL. LabCorp test 004226 (ECLIA): women 20 to 30 years 13 to 71; 31 to 40 years 8 to 60; 41 to 60 years 4 to 50 ng/dL.

analytes.origin: The laboratory pages do not state the population underlying the female interval. Published female reference intervals derive from Haring et al. (2012), using LC-MS/MS in 985 women aged 20 to 80 from one German cohort (2.5th to 97.5th percentile 0.35 to 1.97 nmol/L, about 10 to 57 ng/dL, declining with age) [S3], and Braunstein et al. (2011), using immunoassay in 161 normally cycling women aged 18 to 49 (5th to 95th percentile 15 to 46 ng/dL at age 30 years) [S4]. The Endocrine Society 2007 assay statement calls for normative values “for both genders and children” to be established only after assay standardisation [S7].

sexSpecific.what: Lower reference limit of the adult reference interval by sex (ARUP, LC-MS/MS). No guideline defines a threshold for “low testosterone” in women: “No cutoff blood level can be used for any measured circulating androgen to differentiate women with and without sexual dysfunction” [S6].

contested.summary: A global consensus statement holds that “Direct assays for the measurement of total and free testosterone are highly unreliable in the female range” (Grade A), whereas LC-MS/MS measures “with high accuracy and reproducibility” [S6]. The LabCorp female interval is produced on a direct electrochemiluminescence immunoassay [S2], and ARUP reports no female interval for its immunoassay [S1b]. The published reference intervals rest on 985 women [S3] and 161 women [S4]. The Endocrine Society 2014 guideline states: “We recommend against making a clinical diagnosis of androgen deficiency syndrome in healthy women”, citing “a lack of a well-defined syndrome” and “the lack of valid reference ranges for women” [S5].

analytes.guidanceInBand: A global consensus statement holds that “A blood total testosterone level should not be used to diagnose HSDD” (hypoactive sexual desire disorder) [S6]. The Endocrine Society states: “We recommend against making a clinical diagnosis of androgen deficiency syndrome in healthy women” [S5]. Where testosterone is prescribed, “Dosing should be limited to achieving testosterone concentrations in the physiologic premenopausal range” [S6].

analytes.name: AMH (anti-Müllerian hormone)

labRange.source: LabCorp test 500183 (electrochemiluminescence), women: 20 to 25 years 1.23 to 11.51; 26 to 30 years 1.03 to 11.10; 31 to 35 years 0.66 to 8.75; 36 to 40 years 0.42 to 8.34; 41 to 46 years 0.26 to 5.81; 47 to 54 years ≤0.82; 55 years and over ≤0.18 ng/mL. ARUP test 2002656 (ELISA): 18 to 29 years 0.401 to 16.015; 30 to 39 years 0.176 to 11.705; 40 to 45 years ≤6.282 ng/mL.

analytes.origin: The laboratory pages report age-banded percentiles without naming the population; the lower reference limits of the two laboratories for women aged 30 to 35 differ about fourfold (0.66 and 0.176 ng/mL) [S1, S2]. Values are method-specific because no international standard existed: in the 2020 study by the WHO and the National Institute for Biological Standards and Control, the candidate reagent 16/190 was commutable for 6 methods, partially commutable for 3 and non-commutable for 7 of 16 valid methods, and the WHO established it as a Reference Reagent only [S3].

sexSpecific.what: Reference intervals are female-specific and age-specific by construction; no guideline defines a fertility threshold. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists states that a single AMH measurement “should not be used for counseling patients in this regard” (time to pregnancy) outside infertility care [S4].

contested.summary: Steiner et al. (2017) studied 750 women aged 30 to 44 with no history of infertility: at AMH below 0.7 ng/mL (n = 84) and at 0.7 to 8.4 ng/mL, the probability of conception was, respectively, 65% (95% CI 50 to 75) and 62% (57 to 66) by 6 cycles and 84% (70 to 91) and 75% (70 to 79) by 12 cycles; the adjusted hazard ratio was 1.19 (0.88 to 1.61). Low AMH values “were not associated with reduced fertility” [S6]. Laboratories nonetheless mark values below the age-specific interval as low, and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists issued an opinion addressing women “not seeking fertility care” [S4]; 7 of 16 assay methods are non-commutable with the WHO reagent [S3].

analytes.guidanceInBand: Committee Opinion 773 of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists states that AMH “should not be used for counseling patients in this regard” (time to pregnancy) and that routine testing to predict pregnancy loss “is not recommended” [S4]. The American Society for Reproductive Medicine (2020) states that ovarian-reserve markers “are weak predictors of reproductive potential when age is taken into account” [S5].

analytes.name: Prolactin

labRange.source: ARUP test 0070115 (chemiluminescent immunoassay, 10 years and over); LabCorp test 004465 reports female 13 to 50 years 4.8 to 33.4 ng/mL and male 31 to 50 years 3.9 to 22.7 ng/mL.

analytes.origin: The intervals derive from manufacturer reference-interval studies (LabCorp cites the Roche package insert) [S2]; the population is not described. The Endocrine Society 2011 guideline states: “Assay-specific normal values are higher in women than in men and are generally lower than 25 μg/liter” [S3].

sexSpecific.what: Upper reference limit of the adult reference interval (ARUP). ARUP also reports 9.7 to >200 ng/mL in pregnancy and 1.8 to 20.3 ng/mL in postmenopausal women [S1].

contested.summary: Macroprolactin, a biologically inactive prolactin-IgG complex, is detected by immunoassays: “All prolactin assays currently available are affected with 5-25% of results” indicating hyperprolactinaemia being falsely elevated [S4]. Suliman et al. (2003) identified 21 women in whom hyperprolactinaemia (above 1000 mIU/L) was “accounted for entirely by the presence of macroprolactin”; pituitary imaging had been performed in 93% and dopamine agonists prescribed in 87% [S5].

analytes.guidanceInBand: Recommendation 1.1 of the Endocrine Society 2011 guideline states that “a level above the upper limit of normal confirms the diagnosis as long as the serum sample was obtained without excessive venipuncture stress”; Recommendation 1.2 states: “In patients with asymptomatic hyperprolactinemia, we suggest assessing for macroprolactin” [S3].

analytes.name: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)

labRange.source: LabCorp test 001503 (ECLIA).

analytes.origin: The interval is that of the manufacturer. The historical decision threshold, “commonly set in the region of 200 ng/L (148 pmol/L)”, derives partly from older radioassay and microbiological methods rather than current assays [S3]; the British Society for Haematology 2014 guideline states that thresholds cannot be standardised across methods and recommends local reference intervals [S4].

sexSpecific.what: No sex-specific threshold was identified; pregnancy is treated as an interpretive exception, without a verified numeric threshold [S3].

contested.summary: Harrington et al. state: “There is no gold standard test for deficiency” [S3]. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guideline NG239 (2024) “suggests an indeterminate range of 180 to 350 ng/L (133 to 258 pmol/L)”, with methylmalonic acid measurement for symptomatic people [S3]; a UK survey found that 16.6% of laboratories used the NG239 threshold of 180 ng/L and that reported thresholds ranged from 65 to 239 ng/L [S5]. The LabCorp lower reference limit (232 pg/mL) falls within that indeterminate range [S1].

analytes.guidanceInBand: Guideline NG239, as described by Harrington et al. (2025), states: “MMA measurement should be considered in people who have symptoms or signs of B12 deficiency” (MMA: methylmalonic acid) [S3]. The British Society for Haematology 2014 guideline states that treatment should not be delayed when clinical features strongly suggest deficiency but test results disagree [S4].
